outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Real-Axis Projection of a Phasor
outline_section.learning_goal: Teach that a phasor's real-axis projection is its real part, so a phasor of magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$ projects to $A\cos\theta$ and a rotating phasor gives $x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Establish that the real-axis projection of a phasor is its real part, so a phasor with magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$ has projection $A\cos\theta$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a unit phasor on the positive real axis, then move to a phasor of magnitude $A$ at a general angle $\theta$.
paragraph_plan: Connect this lesson to the previous phasor topics by stating that the tip of the phasor moves in the complex plane and that the real-axis shadow is the cosine-valued signal we want.
Begin with a fixed phasor and show that its real-axis projection is the adjacent-side component, so the projection equals $A\cos\theta$.
State the same rule in complex-number language by taking the real part of $A e^{j\theta}$.
Replace the fixed angle with a time-dependent angle $\theta(t)=\omega t+\phi$ for counterclockwise rotation.
Summarize the bridge from phasor geometry to the time-domain cosine and preview that later sections vary only rotation direction and evaluation time.
